messages:
lee: quick sync request — we need a decision on how the policy engine resolves ties when multiple routing policies match a request (eg. low-latency tier vs low-cost tier vs region-preferred). do we: 1) hard constraints first then scoring, 2) merged weighted score, or 3) deterministic priority list maintained per-tenant? thoughts?

nora: +1 to hard constraints first. if a policy says region==eu, that should be a filter not a score. scoring after filtering seems simpler.

sam: cautious — evaluating full filter+score for every request might be expensive at high QPS. we should precompile policy chains into a compact decision DAG and cache it per-tenant. that gives O(1) per-request decision.

maria: agree with both. what about per-tenant overrides? i.e. global default = hard-constraints-then-score, but tenant can define priority weights. example config idea: 

```yaml
policies:
  - id: low_latency
    constraints: [region: us, tier: premium]
    score: {latency_weight: 0.7, cost_weight: 0.3}
  - id: low_cost
    constraints: []
    score: {latency_weight: 0.2, cost_weight: 0.8}
resolution: hard_constraints_then_score
```

maria: this keeps semantics clear and lets optimize the common case.

joel: small nit — deterministic tie-breakers matter. if two policies have equal score we need a stable rule. random selection can be okay for load spread but hurts reproducibility and debugging. propose: 1) stable hash-based tiebreak seeded by request id for load spread but reproducible, 2) ability to opt into deterministic ordering for debuggability.

lee: good call. so combine: hard constraints -> compute score -> if tie within epsilon use hash-based deterministic tiebreak (seed=request.id). keeps both spread + reproducible.

sam: on the precompile idea — if we precompute per-tenant decision DAG, we also need a fast path for policy updates (rollouts). can we do incremental compile and atomic swap? sketches: compile->validate->publish new DAG, workers swap pointer. uses minimal downtime.

nora: +1. rollout behavior should include canary fraction and fallback. e.g. new routing policy activated for 5% of traffic for 1h, if error rate or latency regressions detected auto rollback. ties into observability.

maria: monitoring checklist: per-policy QPS, median p95 latency, error-rate, cost-per-token delta. also alerts when scoring distribution shifts significantly.

joel: also think about constraint expressiveness. we currently allow simple equals and set membership. customers will ask for geo-fallback chains (prefer eu, then global) and capacity-aware constraints (only route if node.capacity>threshold). capacity check requires real-time signals — that complicates precompile. maybe treat capacity as soft score with very high weight instead of hard constraint.

lee: summary proposal: 
- constraint-first evaluation for static constraints (region, tier, customer flags)
- scoring phase for soft signals (latency, cost, utilization)
- deterministic hash tiebreak seeded by request id within an epsilon threshold
- per-tenant compiled decision DAG cached on workers, with atomic swap on publish
- rollout primitives: canary fraction + automated rollback on SLO regressions
- keep capacity signals as high-weight scores to avoid runtime coupling to infra metrics

lee: anyone object to that approach? if none, i'll make a short RFC patch and a follow-up PR for the compiler sketch and metrics we need.

sam: sounds good. add an opt-in 'strict-deterministic' flag for customers who need reproducible routing for debugging, and a 'spread' mode that uses the hash as described.

nora: also add unit tests around epsilon tie thresholds and determinism. tiny flakey thresholds will bite us.

maria: i'll draft the example config and some migration notes for existing tenants.

infra-bot: deploy:build triggered by lee — pipeline 4821 queued. :gear:

joel: thanks all. we should also document fallback semantics clearly in the console UI (why a request landed in a cheaper model). transparency reduces ops noise.

lee: agreed. i'll open the RFC PR today and link here. thanks everyone. :thumbsup:
